questions.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 12\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}52 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)={(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b)}^{T}(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=\frac{1}{2}Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b)=\frac{1}{2}A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}A)}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{1}{2}A)}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & ={A}^{T}(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{T}(\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}16 \\ 34\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}8 \\ 17\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}62 \\ 45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-2 \\ 2-2 \\ 2-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4+0-3 \\ -3+0+2 \\ -3+0+4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+0+0 \\ 0+0+0 \\ 1+0+0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
